about: The course's lectures, each in a topic family that colours its cards, each with the labs it teaches, then the words of each lab and its practice questions. Lecture numbers, dates and titles are those on each lecture file's first slide. Answers are the course's own; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.title: Advanced Arduino programming
lectures.note: The file is named les9; its first slide says Lesson 8.

labs.title: Ohm's law
labs.idea: Push harder (more voltage) and more current flows; narrow the pipe (more resistance) and less flows.
labs.law: U = I × R    P = U × I
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 1 (28 Sep), slides 37–44; lesson 2, slides 13 and 19 (power)

practice.question: A 12 V battery feeds a 3 Ω lamp. What current flows?
practice.source: EAVP lesson 1, slide 41 (question); answer worked by hand

practice.question: A 200 Ω resistor is connected to 4.5 V. What current flows?
A device takes 2 W from 12 V. What is its resistance?

labs.title: Series and parallel
labs.idea: In series the same current flows through each resistor and the voltages add; in parallel each resistor has the same voltage and the currents add.
labs.law: Series: R = R1 + R2 + …    Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 1, slides 45–53; syllabus §2.4 (the table method); exercises 5 and 6

practice.question: 9 V over 3 kΩ, 10 kΩ and 5 kΩ in series. What voltage stands across the 10 kΩ?
practice.source: EAVP syllabus §2.4, table method, series example; lesson 1, slides 46–48

practice.question: Four 3 Ω heating elements on 12 V. Wired as two parallel pairs in series, what power do they give?
practice.solution: Each pair: 3 ∥ 3 = 1.5 Ω. Two pairs in series: 3 Ω. P = U² / R = 144 / 3 = 48 W.

practice.question: 6 Ω, 12 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel. What is the total resistance?

labs.title: Voltage divider
labs.idea: Two resistors in series share the supply voltage in proportion to their size. A potentiometer is a divider you turn; a light sensor is one whose lower resistor changes with light.
labs.law: Uout = Uin × R2 / (R1 + R2)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 1, slides 45–49 (series); exercise 2; lesson 5 and 8 (Grove potentiometer and light sensor)

practice.question: R1 = 110 Ω and R2 in series on 12 V; 4 V stands across R1. What is R2?

labs.title: LED series resistor
labs.idea: An LED keeps about the same voltage across it whatever you do; the resistor takes the rest and sets the current.
labs.law: R = (Usupply − ULED) / I
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 3, slide 26 (an LED does not follow Ohm's law); lesson 5 (220 or 330 Ω); exercise 11

practice.question: An LED of 2 V at 20 mA on a 5 V Arduino pin. What series resistor?
practice.solution: R = (5 − 2) V / 0.02 A = 150 Ω. It dissipates P = 3 V × 0.02 A = 0.06 W.

labs.title: Long cables
labs.idea: A wire is a resistor too. A long, thin cable takes part of the voltage before it reaches the load, and turns it into heat.
labs.law: R = ρ × l / A    loss = I × R per wire, two wires
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 2, slides 21–27 (Pouillet); syllabus §2.8; exercise 9; example exam question 5

practice.question: A load 700 m away draws 25 A from 230 V and needs 220 V, so each copper wire may drop 5 V. What cross-section is needed (in mm²)?

labs.title: Electric shock
labs.idea: Your body is a resistor. The voltage you touch and how well you are insulated decide the current, and the current decides the harm.
labs.law: I = U / Rbody
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 4, slides 7–8 (danger of currents, resistance of the body); slides 16–21 (the 30 mA differential breaker)

practice.question: You stand in a damp room (about 5 kΩ) and touch 230 V. What current flows through you?
practice.solution: I = 230 V / 5 kΩ = 46 mA. On AC that is above 30 mA: extreme pain, risk of cardiac arrest. A 30 mA differential breaker trips.
practice.source: Body resistance and AC table: EAVP lesson 4, slides 7–8; answer worked by hand

labs.title: Transformer
labs.idea: Two coils on one iron core. The ratio of their windings sets the ratio of the voltages; the power stays the same, so where the voltage goes up the current goes down. Only for AC.
labs.law: Uin / Uout = Nin / Nout    Uin × Iin = Uout × Iout
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 3, slides 20–23; lesson 4 (distribution); exercise 10

practice.question: A transformer with 80 windings on the mains side and 20 on the lamp side feeds a 20 Ω lamp from 230 V. What voltage stands across the lamp?
practice.solution: Uout = 230 V × 20 / 80 = 57.5 V. The lamp then takes P = 57.5² / 20 ≈ 165 W.

labs.title: Battery life
labs.idea: Capacity in Ah is current times time. Multiply by the voltage and you have the energy in Wh.
labs.law: I = P / U    Ah = I × t    Wh = Ah × U
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 2, slides 28–36; lesson 12 (batteries); example exam question 3

practice.question: A 3 W LED lamp on a 7.4 V LiPo must shine 16 h. How many Ah does the battery need?
A phone battery of 3.7 V and 3500 mAh. How much energy is one full charge?
practice.solution: Wh = 3.5 Ah × 3.7 V = 12.95 Wh. Two hundred charges: 2.59 kWh; at €0.50 per kWh, €1.30.

labs.title: From AC to smooth DC
labs.idea: A diode lets current pass one way only. One diode keeps half of each wave; a Graetz bridge of four turns the negative halves round. A capacitor fills the gaps; the load empties it between the peaks.
labs.law: Half wave: one diode    Full wave: Graetz bridge    Smoothing: a capacitor across the load
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 10, p. 6–9 (diode, Graetz bridge, smoothing); example exam question 2

labs.title: From voltage to analogRead
labs.idea: The Arduino measures a voltage between 0 and 5 V and gives a whole number: 10 bits, so 2¹⁰ = 1024 steps, 0 to 1023. map() turns that number into what you need, such as a servo angle.
labs.law: value = U / 5 V × 1024 (whole steps)    angle = map(value, 0, 1023, 0, 180)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 5, slides 40 and 51 (10-bit ADC); example jury question 2; lesson 11 (ADC and DAC)

practice.question: A potentiometer gives 2.5 V on A0. Which angle does map(analogRead(A0), 0, 1023, 0, 180) give?
practice.source: Worked by hand from the definitions of analogRead and map (example jury question 2 asks for the same chain)

labs.title: PWM: a voltage by switching
labs.idea: A digital pin is only 0 V or 5 V. Switch it fast, and the time it is high sets the average: an LED looks dimmer, a motor turns slower.
labs.law: average = duty × 5 V    duty = value / 255
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 5, slide 54 (U = Ton / (Ton + Toff) × Vcc); lesson 10, p. 17 (PWM)

practice.question: analogWrite(pin, 51) on a 5 V Arduino. What is the average voltage?
practice.source: Worked by hand from the definition of analogWrite (8 bits, 0–255)

labs.title: Binary numbers
labs.idea: A digital circuit only knows 0 and 1. Each place is worth twice the one to its right. Negative numbers: invert every bit and add 1.
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 11, p. 6–17 (number systems, two's complement); p. 53–55 (flash ADC)

practice.question: What is 11010 in binary as a decimal number?
Which number is 1011 in 4-bit two's complement?
practice.solution: The first bit is 1, so it is negative. Invert: 0100, add 1: 0101 = 5. So 1011 = −5.

practice.question: How many comparators does an 8-bit flash ADC need?

labs.title: Sizing a motor
labs.idea: Power is force times speed. Work out the ideal power, then design for the worst case with a margin: a motor should not run at its limit.
labs.law: P = F × v    F = m × g (g ≈ 10 m/s²)    v = h / t
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 13, p. 24–29 (choosing a motor; the garage door)

practice.question: A garage door motor must lift 30 kg by 2.5 m in 30 s. What power is that, ideally?
practice.solution: F = 30 kg × 10 m/s² = 300 N; v = 2.5 m / 30 s = 0.083 m/s; P = 300 × 0.083 = 25 W. With 60 kg, acceleration and friction the lesson takes about 100 W.

labs.title: Measuring U and I
labs.idea: An ammeter has almost no resistance and goes in series, in the path of the current. A voltmeter has a very high resistance and goes in parallel, across the part. Swap them and the circuit shows you.
labs.law: Ammeter: in series, low R    Voltmeter: in parallel, high R
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 3, slides 6–13 (meters); exercises 3 and 8

practice.question: Two equal resistors in parallel on a battery. The battery supplies 1 A and the voltmeter across R2 reads 2 V. What is R2?
practice.solution: Equal resistors share the current: 0.5 A each. R2 = 2 V / 0.5 A = 4 Ω.

labs.title: RMS and peak
labs.idea: Mains voltage swings up and down 50 times a second. Its RMS value is the DC voltage that would heat a resistor just as much; the peak is √2 times higher.
labs.law: Upeak = √2 × URMS
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 4, slide 12

practice.question: The mains is 230 V RMS. What is its peak voltage?
practice.source: Formula: EAVP lesson 4, slide 12; answer worked by hand

labs.title: Pull-down resistor
labs.idea: A pin connected to nothing has no level: it reads whatever it picks up. A resistor to GND (pull-down) or to 5 V (pull-up) holds it at a defined level until the button changes it.
labs.law: Open: pin pulled to GND through R → LOW    Pressed: pin at 5 V → HIGH
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 5, slides 42–44 (digital input, pull-down 10 kΩ)

practice.question: A button to 5 V and a 10 kΩ pull-down on D2. While it is pressed, what current flows through the resistor?
practice.solution: The pin node is at 5 V, so I = 5 V / 10 kΩ = 0.5 mA: small, as the slide says.
practice.source: Circuit: EAVP lesson 5, slides 42–44; answer worked by hand

labs.title: Temperature sensor (NTC)
labs.idea: An NTC is a resistor that drops as it warms. Put it in a divider and the temperature becomes a voltage the Arduino can read.
labs.law: Uout = 5 V × Rfixed / (RNTC + Rfixed)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 8 (sensors: the NTC and its table)

practice.question: The lecture's NTC (11.75 kΩ at 5 °C) above a 4.7 kΩ fixed resistor on 5 V. What voltage reaches A0?
practice.source: NTC table: EAVP lesson 8; answer worked by hand

labs.title: Opamp amplifier
labs.idea: An opamp amplifies the difference between its two inputs. Equal inputs give nothing, however large; a small difference gives a large output, as far as the supply allows.
labs.law: Vout = Av × (V+ − V−)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 10, p. 13 (amplifier, the gain-4 table)

practice.question: Gain 4, −3 V on the minus input and 3 V on the plus input. What is the output?
practice.source: EAVP lesson 10, p. 13, the table's ninth column

labs.title: Button bounce
labs.idea: A button's contacts spring open and shut a few times as they meet. The Arduino is fast enough to see every one: one press counts as several. Waiting until the reading is steady fixes it.
labs.law: Accept a change only when steady for longer than debounceDelay (50 ms)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 11, p. 35–37 (contact bounce, debouncing with Arduino)

labs.title: Real batteries
labs.idea: Cells in series add their voltages; in parallel they keep the voltage and share the current. Every cell has a little resistance inside, so the voltage at the load sags as the load draws more.
labs.law: Series: E = n × Ecell    Parallel: E = Ecell    U = E − I × r
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 2, slides 28–36 (batteries; non-ideal battery)

practice.question: A 10 V battery with 0.2 Ω inside feeds a 1 Ω load. What voltage reaches the load?
practice.solution: I = 10 V / (0.2 + 1) Ω = 8.33 A; U = 8.33 A × 1 Ω = 8.33 V. The other 1.67 V stays inside the battery.

labs.title: Energy bill
labs.idea: Energy is power times time; the bill is energy times price. For heating, a heat pump gives three times the heat it takes as electricity, which can beat cheaper gas.
labs.law: E [kWh] = P [kW] × t [h]    cost = E × price
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 3, slide 25; lesson 4, slides 24–26 (consumption analysis); exercise 10

practice.question: A lamp of 165.3 W burns for a whole day. How much energy is that, in kWh?
practice.solution: E = 0.1653 kW × 24 h = 3.97 kWh, about 4 kWh; at €0.25 per kWh, €1.

labs.title: Lowering a voltage
labs.idea: A linear regulator such as the LM7805 turns the excess voltage into heat; a series resistor does the same, worse. Switching the voltage on and off fast (PWM) loses little.
labs.law: Heat = (Uin − Uout) × I    efficiency = Uout / Uin
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 10, p. 17–19 (DC to DC conversion); exercise 7

practice.question: A 400 Ω motor needs 150 V but the mains gives 230 V. Which series resistor drops the rest?
practice.solution: I = 150 V / 400 Ω = 0.375 A. The resistor takes 80 V: R = 80 V / 0.375 A = 213.33 Ω, burning 30 W.

labs.title: Logic gates
labs.idea: A gate turns one or two inputs, each 0 or 1, into one output by a fixed rule: its truth table. In an Arduino sketch the same rules are !, && and ||.
labs.law: AND: both    OR: at least one    NOT: the opposite    XOR: exactly one
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 11, p. 19–28 (logic gates)

practice.question: A NAND gate gets 1 on both inputs. What is its output (0 or 1)?
practice.solution: AND of 1 and 1 is 1; NAND is NOT AND, so 0.

labs.title: From number to voltage (DAC)
labs.idea: A DAC does the opposite of analogRead: it turns a binary number into a voltage. Each bit pushes current through a resistor twice as large as the one before; an opamp adds them.
labs.law: Vout = −Rf × (U1/R + U2/2R + U3/4R)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 11, p. 50–52 (R/2nR DAC)

practice.question: The lecture's DAC with an 800 Ω feedback resistor (R = 1 kΩ, 5 V logic). What does code 111 give?

labs.title: Battery budget
labs.idea: A sensor node sleeps most of the time and wakes to measure and send. Add up the mAh of each state over a year, and the battery's capacity tells you how long it lasts.
labs.law: mAh per year = mA × seconds × times a day × 365 / 3600    life = capacity / mAh per year
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 12, p. 19–20 (IoT device examples)

practice.question: The lecture's sensor node uses 2686.4 mAh a year. How many years does a 5200 mAh battery last?

labs.title: The breadboard
labs.idea: Inside a breadboard, metal strips join holes in groups of five. Two legs in one strip are joined to each other, so a part placed that way does nothing: it is shorted.
labs.law: a–e of one column: one strip    f–j: another    rails: the whole length
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 5 (the breadboard; the button and LED exercises)

labs.title: Using a multimeter
labs.idea: A multimeter has a socket for each job and a range for each size. Black lead in COM; red in V for voltage, in mA or A for current; start at the highest range.
labs.law: U: red in V, across the part    I: red in mA or A, in series
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 3, slides 10–13 (multimeter, scale indication, meters in practice)

labs.title: Transistor as a switch
labs.idea: A small current into the base lets a large current flow from collector to emitter. The Arduino's pin gives the small one; the transistor and its own supply handle the large one.
labs.law: Ib = (5 V − 0.7 V) / Rb    Ic ≤ β × Ib
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 10, p. 11 (transistor); Arduino lesson of 5 Nov, p. 28–33 (NPN, LED strip with transistor)

practice.question: Pin 9 at 5 V drives an NPN transistor through 220 Ω, with 0.7 V across its base. What base current flows?
practice.solution: Ib = (5 − 0.7) V / 220 Ω = 19.5 mA. That is more than the UNO R4's 8 mA per pin from lesson 5: a larger resistor, such as 1 kΩ, is kinder to the pin.
practice.source: Circuit: EAVP Arduino lesson of 5 Nov, p. 31; answer worked by hand

labs.title: Shift register
labs.idea: A 74HC595 takes bits one at a time on a single data pin, each with a clock pulse, and shows all eight at once when latched: eight outputs from three pins.
labs.law: shiftOut(dataPin, clockPin, MSBFIRST, data)
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 11, p. 40–46 (shift registers); Arduino lesson of 5 Nov, p. 34–37 (74HC595)

practice.question: Two 74HC595s chained, Q7S of the first to the data input of the second. How many outputs do the three Arduino pins drive?
practice.solution: Each 74HC595 has 8 outputs; chained they share data, clock and latch: 2 × 8 = 16.
practice.source: EAVP Arduino lesson of 5 Nov, p. 37

labs.title: Mixing colours
labs.idea: A NeoPixel holds a red, a green and a blue LED, each dimmed from 0 to 255. Light adds up: red and green give yellow, all three give white.
labs.law: colour = (red, green, blue), each 0–255    256³ colours
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 9 (4 Nov), NeoPixel and NeoMatrix; Arduino lesson of 5 Nov, p. 3–12

practice.question: How many colours can a NeoPixel make with three channels of 0 to 255?

labs.title: Variable types and overflow
labs.idea: A whole-number variable has a fixed number of bits. Past its largest value it wraps round to its smallest, without any warning; dividing two whole numbers drops the decimals.
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 7 (variable types); lesson 9 (typecasting); lecture 13, p. 30–35 (the Boeing 787)

practice.question: On an UNO R3, int x = 32767; x = x + 1; What is x now?
practice.solution: An int on the R3 is 16 bits, −32 768 to 32 767. One more wraps round to −32 768.
practice.source: Range: EAVP lesson 7, the type table; answer by definition

labs.title: Number bases
labs.idea: The same number can be written in base 10, 2, 8 or 16. Hexadecimal is binary in groups of four bits, octal in groups of three. Adding in binary works like decimal: 1 + 1 = 10, carry the 1.
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 11, p. 6–16 (numbering systems, conversions, binary arithmetic)

practice.question: What is the hexadecimal number 1A in decimal?

labs.title: Stepper or servo
labs.idea: A stepper turns a fixed angle per step and counts steps, but cannot see where it is: under too much load it skips steps and never knows. A servo measures its angle and corrects itself.
labs.law: Stepper: angle = steps × 1.8°    Servo: goes to the angle it is told (0–180°)
labs.lecture: EAVP lecture 13, p. 18–26 (stepper, servo, servo versus stepper); Arduino lesson of 5 Nov, p. 21–24

practice.question: A stepper of 1.8° per step. How many steps make one full turn?
practice.source: Step angle: EAVP lecture 13, p. 26; answer worked by hand

labs.title: State machine
labs.idea: A traffic light is always in one state. An event, here its time running out, moves it to the next. Writing a sketch this way keeps it from waiting with delay(), so it can still react to a button.
labs.law: states + events + transitions
labs.lecture: EAVP lesson 9 (4 Nov), finite state machines: the traffic light

practice.question: Green 5 s, orange 2 s, red 5 s. How long is one full cycle of the traffic light?
practice.source: EAVP lesson 9, the traffic light example

labs.title: Battery chemistries
labs.idea: Each battery chemistry has its own cell voltage, and those voltages are asked by heart at the exam. Cells in series reach a higher voltage; a LiPo must stay between 3.2 and 4.2 V.
labs.law: Alkaline 1.5 V · NiCd 1.2 V · NiMH 1.2 V · lead-acid 2 V · Li-ion/LiPo 3.6–3.7 V
labs.lecture: EAVP lecture 12, p. 3–13 (battery types, LiPo safety, overview table); lesson 2 (car battery)

practice.question: A 12 V car battery is built from lead-acid cells. How many cells does it hold?
practice.solution: 12 V / 2 V per cell = 6 cells in series.
practice.source: EAVP lesson 2 (a car battery is 6 × 2.0 V); lecture 12, p. 8
